props.title: Exam

sections.content: Exam (2009) masterfully demonstrates how to create intense psychological tension in a single room. Like 12 Angry Men (1957) and Cube (1997), it strips away external distractions to focus purely on human nature under pressure. Director Stuart Hazeldine crafts a pressure-cooker environment where eight candidates compete for a mysterious corporate position, each given 80 minutes to answer one question - except the question itself becomes the maddening puzzle. The film shares DNA with other mind-game thrillers like Fermat's Room (2007) and Circle (2015), where intellectual challenges become matters of life and death.

sections.content: The genius of Exam lies in how it peels back layers of civility to expose raw human nature. Like The Belko Experiment (2016) and Would You Rather (2012), it forces characters to choose between cooperation and competition. The stark white examination room becomes a psychological battlefield where alliances form and shatter. The film's minimalist approach - one room, eight characters, real-time progression - amplifies every gesture and word, creating suffocating tension without any traditional action sequences.

The corporate thriller elements in Exam connect it to films like The Game (1997) and Platform (2019), where mysterious organizations orchestrate elaborate tests of human character. The film's commentary on corporate culture and power dynamics feels especially relevant alongside works like Sorry to Bother You (2018) and Mayhem (2017), which use genre elements to critique modern workplace dynamics. sections.content: Exam belongs to a sophisticated wave of single-location thrillers that emerged in the late 2000s, including Buried (2010) and Phone Booth (2002). These films prove that spatial restriction can enhance rather than limit storytelling possibilities. The claustrophobic setting becomes a pressure cooker for character development, forcing confrontations that might feel contrived in a larger space. This approach has influenced later works like 10 Cloverfield Lane (2016) and The Platform (2019).
